645.title: Rosh Hashanah: kingship, memory, shofar
645.hook: the extra service has three parts: God as king, God remembering, the shofar
645.howItsDone: In the Rosh Hashanah Musaf, the prayer leader recites Malchuyot, Zichronot and Shofarot, each with ten verses, and in many synagogues the shofar is sounded after each; many congregations kneel and bow to the floor at Aleinu.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the world's birthday. Your line was happy birthday, world. Did a stranger get treated like it was their day? Today, the heart of the Rosh Hashanah service, in three parts. Day six hundred forty-five.

On most Shabbats and festivals, the additional Amidah, the Musaf, has seven blessings. On Rosh Hashanah it has nine. The three in the middle are each built like a small anthology: ten verses, chosen from across the Bible, stitched into a prayer, and followed, in many synagogues, by the shofar. If you've ever sat through a Rosh Hashanah service and wondered why it's so long, this is a big part of the answer.
screen: `SEVEN BLESSINGS BECOME NINE.` → `TEN VERSES EACH.` → `WHY IT'S SO LONG.`

segments.voice: The three middle blessings are Malchuyot, kingship. Zichronot, remembrances. And Shofarot, the shofar. The Talmud, in Rosh Hashanah 16a, explains them as if God were speaking: say before Me kingships, so that you make Me king over you. Remembrances, so that your memory rises before Me for good. And how? With the shofar. The Mishnah asks for ten verses for each. In the prayer book they're drawn from the Torah, the Writings and the Prophets, ending with the Torah again. In Malchuyot, one of them comes from the Song of the Sea: "The LORD shall reign for ever and ever." The prayer that opens Malchuyot is Aleinu, the one we met at the end of every daily service, our duty to praise. Tradition says it began here, as the introduction to kingship on Rosh Hashanah, and only later moved into the everyday. On Rosh Hashanah, when the words come to we bend the knee, many congregations don't just bow. They kneel, and bow to the floor. Why start the new year with kingship? Because a king, in the old world, was the one whose word ruled your days. To say God is king is to ask: what actually rules my life? My phone. My fear. My boss. The approval of people I don't even like. Malchuyot is a yearly audit of loyalties. Before the tradition asks God to remember you, it asks you to decide whom you serve.
screen: `KINGSHIP, MEMORY, SHOFAR.` · `MAKE ME KING OVER YOU.` · `TEN VERSES, THREE KINDS OF BOOK.` · `ALEINU BEGAN HERE.` · then, large: `WHO IS KING?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name what rules your life. Sit, and be honest. What actually sets your schedule, your mood, your choices? Name two or three things, without judging them. Some may be good: a child, a calling. Some may not be. Now ask: if I could choose, what would I want to rule my days? If you pray, you can say the line from the Song of the Sea: the LORD shall reign. If not, name the value you'd crown. The bell holds the time.
Malchuyot. Kingships. The first of the three great middle blessings of the Rosh Hashanah Musaf, where God is declared king.
Your line: who is king. Today, when something tries to boss your mood, ask: who is king here? Day six hundred forty-five.

646.title: Rosh Hashanah: the three sounds
646.hook: tekiah, shevarim, teruah: one long blast, broken sighs, short sobs
646.howItsDone: On Rosh Hashanah (except on Shabbat) the shofar is sounded in the synagogue in sets of tekiah, shevarim and teruah, a caller announcing each note; many communities reach one hundred blasts over the service.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Malchuyot, kingship, the yearly audit. Your line was who is king. What tried to boss your mood, and did you notice? Today, the sound that the third blessing calls for. Day six hundred forty-six.

Stand in a synagogue on Rosh Hashanah and listen. A man lifts a curved horn to his lips. A caller beside him reads out a word, and he blows. One long, steady note. Then the caller says another word, and the horn makes three broken, wavering notes, like someone catching their breath. Then a third word, and a rapid string of short bursts, almost a stammer. Then one long note again. Three kinds of sound, over and over, and by a custom many keep, a hundred blasts by the end of the day.
screen: `ONE LONG, STEADY NOTE.` → `THREE BROKEN NOTES.` → `A STRING OF SHORT BURSTS.`

segments.voice: The three sounds are tekiah, the long blast; shevarim, the broken notes, from a word meaning breaks; and teruah, the rapid short ones. The Torah calls Rosh Hashanah a day of teruah. But it never describes what a teruah sounds like. So the Talmud, in Rosh Hashanah 33b and 34a, investigates. It notices that the old Aramaic translation renders teruah with a word for crying. And it finds the same root in the Song of Deborah, where Sisera's mother waits at her window for a son who will never come home, and cries. So a teruah is a cry. But what kind? Maybe it's a groan: long, heavy sighs. Maybe it's a wail: short, gasping sobs. Maybe a person does both, sighs and then sobs, the way people really cry. Nobody could be sure which the Torah meant. So the sage Rabbi Abbahu, in Caesarea, set an order that covered every possibility: the sighs alone, the sobs alone, and the sighs followed by the sobs. Each surrounded by a long, steady tekiah before and after. That's why the pattern is so long, and why it adds up to so many blasts. It's an honest admission that the tradition wasn't certain, so it chose to do every version. Notice the frame, too. The broken sounds always sit inside the whole ones. Crying, held on both sides by something steady. Many teachers read it as a picture of the year: the brokenness is real, and it is not the whole story.
screen: `TEKIAH, SHEVARIM, TERUAH.` · `A DAY OF TERUAH, NEVER DESCRIBED.` · `SISERA'S MOTHER AT THE WINDOW.` · `SIGHS, SOBS, OR BOTH.` · then, large: `A SIGH AND A SOB.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: breathe long, broken, short. First, one long, steady breath out, like a tekiah. Then three breaths out in pieces, like sighs. Then a few quick, short breaths, like sobs. Then one long breath again, whole. Repeat the pattern slowly while the bell holds. If something from this year needs a sigh, let it have one. If you pray, the breaths can carry that to God. The long breath at the end is there to hold the rest. The bell holds the time.
Teruah. The broken cry of the shofar, whose exact sound the Torah never describes, so the tradition plays every version.
Your line: a sigh and a sob. Today, when something hard lands, let yourself sigh once, and then breathe one long breath after it. Day six hundred forty-six.

647.title: Rosh Hashanah: Hannah (1 Samuel 1)
647.hook: the haftarah tells of Hannah praying for a child, and being heard
647.tomorrow: Rosh Hashanah: the boy is heard (Genesis 21)
647.howItsDone: On the first day of Rosh Hashanah, after the Torah reading, the haftarah from 1 Samuel 1:1–2:10 is chanted in the synagogue, including Hannah's prayer and her song of thanks.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the three sounds of the shofar. Your line was a sigh and a sob. Did a hard moment get its sigh, and then a long breath? Today, a woman whose prayer the rabbis learned from, read on the new year. Day six hundred forty-seven.

Every year, the family goes up to the sanctuary at Shiloh. Every year, there's a festive meal. And every year, the same scene. Elkanah gives portions of meat to his wife Peninnah and all her sons and daughters. To his other wife, Hannah, whom he loves, he gives a double portion. Because Hannah has no children. And Peninnah, every year, makes sure she feels it. Hannah cries and won't eat. Her husband asks, gently and a bit cluelessly: "am not I better to thee than ten sons?"
screen: `EVERY YEAR, UP TO SHILOH.` → `A DOUBLE PORTION, NO CHILDREN.` → `BETTER THAN TEN SONS?`

segments.voice: This is the haftarah, the prophetic reading, for the first day of Rosh Hashanah: the first chapter of the book of Samuel. Weeks ago we met Hannah's quiet prayer, the lips moving with no voice, which the rabbis made the model for the Amidah. Today, the question is why her story is read on the new year. The Talmud, in Rosh Hashanah 11a, says that on Rosh Hashanah three women were remembered: Sarah, Rachel and Hannah. Three women who had longed for children, and on this day, the tradition says, God remembered them. So on the day the liturgy is full of remembrance, the reading is about a woman who asked to be remembered, almost in those words. Her vow says: if Thou wilt "remember me, and not forget Thy handmaid." Watch what Hannah does in the story. She doesn't argue with Peninnah. She doesn't accept her husband's comfort as an answer. She gets up from the table, goes to the sanctuary, and pours out her soul. And when the priest Eli thinks she's drunk, she corrects him, respectfully and firmly. He blesses her. The text says her face was no more sad. Before anything has changed, she's already lighter. In time, she has a son, Samuel. And here's the turn: she gives him back, bringing him to serve at Shiloh. The next chapter is her song of thanks. It's about reversals: the Lord brings low and lifts up, the barren bears seven. Being heard, for Hannah, began before the answer came. It began with being seen.
screen: `THE FIRST DAY'S HAFTARAH.` · `SARAH, RACHEL AND HANNAH.` · `REMEMBER ME, AND NOT FORGET.` · `HER FACE WAS NO MORE SAD.` · then, large: `HANNAH WAS HEARD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name something you long for. Not a small want. Something you've carried, maybe for years, maybe quietly. Let yourself name it, the way Hannah got up from the table and named hers. If you pray, you can pour it out to God in your own words, silently, lips moving if you like. If you don't, say it to yourself, honestly, without needing an answer. Then notice whether naming it changes how you sit. The bell holds the time.
Rosh Hashanah. The new year, when the first day's reading tells of Hannah, remembered and heard.
Your line: Hannah was heard. Today, really listen to someone who's hurting, the way Eli finally did, and tell them what you heard. Day six hundred forty-seven.

648.title: Rosh Hashanah: the boy is heard (Genesis 21)
648.hook: the first day's reading includes Hagar and Ishmael rescued by a well
648.howItsDone: On the first day of Rosh Hashanah, Genesis 21, Isaac's birth and the rescue of Hagar and Ishmael, is read from the Torah scroll in the synagogue; the second day reads Genesis 22, the binding of Isaac.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the haftarah of Hannah. Your line was Hannah was heard. Whom did you really listen to? Today, the Torah reading of the same morning, and another mother crying. Day six hundred forty-eight.

The desert of Beer-sheba. A woman and her son, sent away from the only home he's known with some bread and a skin of water. The water runs out. The boy weakens. His mother lays him under one of the bushes, then walks away, about a bowshot, and sits down. She can't watch him die. And she lifts up her voice and weeps. On the first morning of Rosh Hashanah, this is the story read aloud from the Torah.
screen: `THE DESERT OF BEER-SHEBA.` → `THE WATER RUNS OUT.` → `A BOWSHOT AWAY, SHE WEEPS.`

segments.voice: Genesis 21 begins with joy: Sarah, at last, gives birth to Isaac. The Talmud links that to Rosh Hashanah too: Sarah was remembered on this day. But the reading doesn't stop at the happy ending. It goes on to Hagar, Sarah's servant, and her son Ishmael, Abraham's firstborn, sent away into the wilderness. And then comes the verse at the center of it all: "And God heard the voice of the lad; and the angel of God called to Hagar out of heaven, and said unto her: 'What aileth thee, Hagar? fear not; for God hath heard the voice of the lad where he is.'" Notice: it's Hagar who weeps aloud, but the verse says God heard the boy. Maybe his own quiet cry. And Ishmael's name means God hears: it was given to him before he was born, when Hagar first fled into the desert. Then God opens her eyes, and she sees a well of water she hadn't seen. The rabbis lingered on the phrase where he is. Rashi, drawing on the midrash, says the angels objected: this boy's descendants will one day cause harm. And God answered: what is he right now? Right now, he's innocent. A person is judged as they are, where they are, today. On the day of judgment, that's the reading. Not who you might become, not what your children might do. Where you are. Ishmael is honored in Muslim tradition as well, as a prophet and an ancestor. Here, in the Jewish reading, he is simply a thirsty boy, and he is heard.
screen: `SARAH REMEMBERED, ISAAC BORN.` · `HAGAR AND ISHMAEL SENT AWAY.` · `WHERE HE IS.` · `A WELL SHE HADN'T SEEN.` · then, large: `GOD HEARS THE BOY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for someone outside your circle. Think of a person, or a group, you don't usually think about. Someone sent away, someone on the other side of a line, someone whose story isn't yours. Picture them where they are, right now: thirsty, tired, or just living their day. If you pray, ask God to hear them, as the boy was heard. If not, wish them a well of water, whatever that means for them. The bell holds the time.
Rosh Hashanah. The new year, when the first day's Torah reading tells of Hagar and Ishmael, and a boy heard where he is.
Your line: God hears the boy. Today, judge one person by who they are right now, not by what you fear they'll become. Day six hundred forty-eight.

649.title: Rosh Hashanah: the books (Rosh Hashanah 16b)
649.hook: the Talmud pictures three books opened on the new year
649.howItsDone: From Rosh Hashanah to Yom Kippur, Jews add lines to the Amidah asking to be remembered and written in the book of life, and greet each other with 'l'shanah tovah tikatevu' and later 'g'mar chatimah tovah.'

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hagar, Ishmael and the well. Your line was God hears the boy. Did you judge someone by who they are right now? Today, the image behind a Rosh Hashanah greeting. Day six hundred forty-nine.

Leaving synagogue on Rosh Hashanah, people don't just say happy new year. They say: l'shanah tovah tikatevu. May you be written for a good year. Cards say it. Text messages say it. After Rosh Hashanah, the greeting shifts: g'mar chatimah tovah, may you be sealed for good. Written. Sealed. It sounds like paperwork. And in a way it is. It comes from a single image in the Talmud, of books lying open in heaven.
screen: `MAY YOU BE WRITTEN.` → `MAY YOU BE SEALED.` → `BOOKS LYING OPEN.`

segments.voice: In Rosh Hashanah 16b, Rabbi Kruspedai says in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: three books are opened on Rosh Hashanah. One for the completely righteous, one for the completely wicked, and one for those in between, the beinonim. The completely righteous are written and sealed at once, for life. The completely wicked are written and sealed at once, for death. And those in between are held, suspended, from Rosh Hashanah until Yom Kippur. If they earn merit, they're written for life. If not, for death. Now be honest: how many people do you know who are completely righteous? Or completely wicked? Almost everyone is in the middle book. That's the point of the image. The middle book is the open one, the one still being written. The ten days ahead are the time for what goes in it. Maimonides, centuries later, turned this into advice. He said a person should see themselves all year as exactly half good and half not, and the whole world the same way. Then any single good act could tip you, and the world, toward life. The prayers on these days pick up the image again and again. Remember us for life, they say, and write us in the book of life. And then they give a reason: for Your sake, living God. The request for life is made to the God of life. It's a frightening image, and it's meant to be. But it's also hopeful. The book isn't closed yet.
screen: `THREE BOOKS ARE OPENED.` · `THE RIGHTEOUS, THE WICKED, THE MIDDLE.` · `HELD UNTIL YOM KIPPUR.` · `ONE ACT CAN TIP THE SCALE.` · then, large: `WRITE US IN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write one line for this year. Find a scrap of paper, or your phone's notes. Write one sentence you'd want in the book about you, a year from now. Not a resolution about the gym. Something like: she was kinder to her brother. He finally called his father. Keep it short. Then sit with it. If you pray, you can ask to be written for a good year. If not, let the line be a direction. The bell holds the time.
Rosh Hashanah. The new year, when the Talmud says three books are opened, and most of us are in the middle one, still being written.
Your line: write us in. Today, do one small thing that belongs in the line you wrote. Day six hundred forty-nine.

650.title: The ten days
650.hook: the days between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur are for making amends
650.howItsDone: During the Ten Days of Repentance, Jews change wording in the Amidah (HaMelech HaKadosh), say Avinu Malkeinu, add selichot, and many seek out people they have wronged to apologize before Yom Kippur.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the three books, and the middle one still open. Your line was write us in. Did you do one thing that belongs in your line? Today, the days when the middle book is still being written. Day six hundred fifty.

There's a particular feeling to the days between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur. The holiday food is in the fridge. Work and school have started again. Life looks ordinary. But people who keep these days describe a hum underneath, like the week before a big exam, or the days before a long-delayed conversation. Small changes show up, too. Words in the daily prayers shift. Someone you haven't heard from in a year calls, a bit awkwardly, to say they're sorry.
screen: `LIFE LOOKS ORDINARY.` → `A HUM UNDERNEATH.` → `AN AWKWARD PHONE CALL.`

segments.voice: These are the aseret yemei teshuvah, the ten days of return, counting Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur themselves. The Talmud, in Rosh Hashanah 18a, reads a verse from Isaiah as being about these days: "Seek ye the LORD while He may be found, call ye upon Him while He is near." While He is near. These are the near days. The daily Amidah changes to match. All year, one blessing ends: the holy God. For these ten days it ends: the holy King. Forget, and in many traditions you go back and say it again. Avinu Malkeinu, our father, our king, is said at many services. Some people take on stricter habits for just these days. And the center of it all is teshuvah, usually translated repentance, though the word means return, turning back. Maimonides lays out what it involves. You recognize what you did wrong. You regret it. You say it out loud, in words, to God. And you resolve not to do it again. And then he gives a test for whether teshuvah is complete. You find yourself in the same situation, with the same temptation, the same person, the same chance, and this time you choose differently. Not because you can't. Because you've changed. That's the work of these days. Not grand gestures. Specific turns, one person, one habit, one sentence. Ten days is not long. Long enough to do something. Short enough that it can't be put off.
screen: `TEN DAYS OF RETURN.` · `SEEK WHILE HE IS NEAR.` · `THE HOLY GOD BECOMES THE HOLY KING.` · `SAME SITUATION, NEW CHOICE.` · then, large: `TEN DAYS TO TURN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: apologize to one person. Sit, and let a face come to mind: someone you hurt this year, in a big way or a small one. Walk through Maimonides' steps quietly. What did I do? Do I regret it? Can I say it in words? What would I do differently? Then draft the first sentence of an apology, the actual words you'd say or text. Keep it simple and specific. If you pray, you can also bring it to God. The bell holds the time.
Aseret yemei teshuvah. The ten days of return, from Rosh Hashanah to Yom Kippur, when the prayers say the holy King.
Your line: ten days to turn. Today, send the apology you drafted, or set a time to say it. Day six hundred fifty.

651.title: The Shabbat of return (Hosea 14:2)
651.hook: the Shabbat between, with Hosea's "Return, O Israel"
651.howItsDone: On the Shabbat between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, the haftarah from Hosea 14 (with additions from Joel or Micah, by custom) is read, and many rabbis give a major sermon on teshuvah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the ten days of return. Your line was ten days to turn. Did the apology get sent, or at least scheduled? Today, the one Shabbat that falls inside those ten days, and the end of a week. Day six hundred fifty-one.

Every year, between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, there's exactly one Shabbat. It has its own name, taken from the first word of its prophetic reading. In many communities the rabbi gives a long sermon that day, all about coming back. In every other way it looks like any other Shabbat: candles, a long meal, an afternoon nap. And the reading itself opens with a single Hebrew word, shuvah. Return.
screen: `ONE SHABBAT BETWEEN.` → `A SERMON ABOUT COMING BACK.` → `SHUVAH: RETURN.`

segments.voice: Shabbat Shuvah is named for the haftarah from the prophet Hosea: "Return, O Israel, unto the LORD thy God; for thou hast stumbled in thine iniquity." Notice the word Hosea chooses. Not you have rebelled, not you are wicked. Stumbled. You tripped. You can get up. Then the next verse gives instructions, and they're surprising: "Take with you words, and return unto the LORD." Not sacrifices, not gold, not a grand gesture. Words. Hosea goes on: instead of bulls, we'll offer the words of our lips. Later rabbis leaned on this verse when the Temple was gone: prayer could stand in for the offerings. And the whole reading ends in tenderness. God promises to heal, to love freely, to be like dew to Israel, so that it blossoms like a lily. Some call this day Shabbat Teshuvah, the Shabbat of repentance. Shuvah is the command form: come back. Much of the Days of Awe speaks the language of a court: judgment, books, seals. Shabbat Shuvah sounds more like a parent standing at the door. You stumbled. Come back. Bring words. That's the whole week, really. Malchuyot asked who is king. The shofar gave us a sigh and a sob. Hannah was heard, and so was a boy in the desert. Three books opened, and ten days to turn. And now, on the day of rest itself, the simplest version of all of it. Return.

Then breathe, and picture dew on grass in the morning. The bell holds the time.
